sentences.text: Leptoceratops was a small dinosaur approximately 2 meters long that possessed a very large head with a strong jaw but lacked horns and possessed only a very reduced frill.
Its skulls are lower and longer than those of Protoceratops and uniquely lack a crest at the back of the skull, while its body structure suggests it was primarily quadrupedal.
Leptoceratops possesses the largest single-rooted teeth of any ceratopsian, whereas ceratopsids have split, double-rooted teeth.
When first described, the tail neural spines of Leptoceratops were the longest known for any ceratopsian.
Fossils from the Hell Creek Formation suggest that Leptoceratops was capable of scratch-digging or burrowing.

The genus Leptoceratops was first described by Barnum Brown in 1914 after two ceratopsian specimens were discovered in 1910 along the Red Deer River in Alberta by an American Museum of Natural History expedition.
Additional fossil material was later found in 1992 in the Hell Creek Formation of Montana by Brig Konecke.
Leptoceratops was a herbivore, likely feeding on the vegetation available in its environment.
It had an efficient bite capable of processing various food types including angiosperms, conifers, and cycads, which dominated the landscape of the Hell Creek Formation.

Leptoceratops had unique teeth among dinosaurs that showed wear patterns driven by a mammal-like jaw rotation during chewing, creating a unique arcing bite path that created curved wear patterns on its teeth.
These teeth exhibit a unique type of tooth-on-tooth wear shared only with Udanoceratops and Archaeoceratops.
A large ridge on the maxilla suggests Leptoceratops had a muscled cheek pouch to help shred large amounts of vegetation.

Leptoceratops was traditionally assumed to be a quadruped, yet it likely moved bipedally at high speeds and quadrupedally when moving slowly, as its forelimbs were long enough to reach the ground upright, enabling a quadrupedal posture.
Leptoceratops is the namesake genus of the family Leptoceratopsidae, although it was originally classified as a primitive ceratopsian outside the family Ceratopsidae.
Leptoceratops lived during the Late Cretaceous period, specifically the Maastrichtian age.
It inhabited a semi-humid floodplain environment with braided streams and small-treed forests.
Fossil material of Leptoceratops was found 75 meters below the Cretaceous-Paleogene boundary in the middle Hell Creek Formation.

It is debated whether Leptoceratops is unrelated to other forms, belongs within Protoceratopsidae, or forms a clade with genera like Montanoceratops and Udanoceratops, while most studies suggest it is outside Protoceratopsidae and Ceratopsidae, though some suggest it may be allied with Ceratopsidae.
It is also debated whether Leptoceratops was as ecologically restricted to cool environments as previously thought, given its presence in coastal plain formations.
